newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-SAMPRAS WINS TOUGHEST GRAND SLAM TITLE.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-SAMPRAS WINS TOUGHEST GRAND SLAM TITLE.

text.p: World number one Pete Sampras won his ninth Grand Slam title on Sunday, crushing Spain's Carlos Moya in the Australian Open final after what he described as the toughest major tournament of his career.

The 25-year-old American outclassed the unseeded Moya in every department, taking the match 6-2 6-3 6-3 before punching the air in triumph and beaming his first smile to the crowd after two tense weeks.
"This is the toughest major I think I've won," Sampras told reporters after lifting his second Australian Open cup. "I played really, really well."
Sampras, who played five sets in the most severe heat of the tournament to survive the fourth round, wasted no time against Moya on another hot day on Centre Court.
Both men started strongly, serving aces in their opening service games, but top seed Sampras broke the nervous Spaniard's serve in the fourth game of the match and never looked back.
Moya could not produce the kind of all-round court game which earned him wins over defending champion Boris Becker and world number two Michael Chang on his way to the final.
Sampras, dominant at the net and baseline, ran Moya around the court like a ball boy before ending the match in 87 minutes. Moya's often lethal serve deserted him.
"He is number one and he showed it today," said Moya, the tournament's cool-headed heart-throb who leapt to nine in the world rankings from 25 with his first Grand Slam final.
"In the final he's almost unbeatable and I couldn't do it."

Sampras's victory takes him a step higher on the podium of tennis greats. In the post-1968 Open era of tennis, only Sweden's Bjorn Borg has won more Grand Slam men's singles titles, with 11 wins from 16 finals.
It also preserves a remarkable win rate in Grand Slam finals, where Sampras has won nine of 11.
He said later he was not consumed by "the numbers" of tennis and that his mind turned at important moments to the death of his coach and mentor, Tim Gullikson, rather than history books.
Gullikson died of a brain tumour last year.
"I thought about it when I woke up today before the match, and I'm sure he's looking down very happy that I fought through some tough matches," he said. "He will always be in my mind...."
Sampras now takes aim at the French Open, the next Grand Slam event on the tennis calendar and the only title missing from the self-effacing American's trophy shelf.
"I'll do whatever I can to get lucky, like I did here this year, to win it," he said.

Sampras rated this championship as tougher than even last year's U.S. Open where he overcame vomiting and dehydration in a quarter-final to beat another Spaniard, Alex Corretja, in a five-setter lasting over four hours. He went on to take his fourth title at Flushing Meadows.

Here, Sampras played in searing heat topping 50 degrees Celsius (122 Fahrenheit) on the court. Medical experts warned players' lives were being put in danger and officials later closed the Centre Court stadium's roof to shut out the sun.
Moya, whose rock-star good looks made him the tournament's pin-up, had never seemed troubled by the heat, riding a wave of support from his mainly female fans into the final.
His defeat on Sunday was not their only disappointment.
Moya drew good-hearted jeers when, during a speech after the match, he thanked his girlfriend for her support.
